patient.name: Darren Fletcher
patient.complaint: Wheeze, chest tightness and a cough that started after a new job
background: Started as a car body-shop spray painter in Croydon 14 months ago
Previously a warehouse worker; no childhood asthma

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' where the job is the clue: spray painter (isocyanates) with late-onset asthma that improves on holiday, builder or shipyard worker (asbestosis, mesothelioma), miner or sandblaster (silicosis, coal worker's pneumoconiosis), farmer (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).

points: Darren, 44, no asthma as a child.
Wheeze, cough and chest tightness for 10 months.
Worse by the end of the working week.
**Much better on a 2-week holiday** in Spain.
Back at work: symptoms return within days.

steps.lead: Darren's symptoms began at a new workplace: an inhaled **workplace exposure** is the likely cause.

steps.q: Which question will tell you most about the cause of Darren's symptoms?
o: Do you have pets at home?
Do your symptoms improve away from work?
Does anyone in your family have asthma?
Have you had a recent cold?
steps.r: Improvement on days off or holiday links symptoms to **work**. The occupational history is critical.

steps.lead: Darren's wheeze plus a clear job link is the pattern: **occupational history is critical**.
Darren is the textbook case: **late-onset asthma** after a new job, better on holiday, in a spray painter exposed to **isocyanates**.

steps.title: Occupational lung diseases: job to diagnosis
head: Disease
Job / exposure
Key feature
Spirometry

steps.lead: Darren's job points to asthma, but a builder or shipyard worker would point to **asbestosis** or **mesothelioma**, and a sandblaster to **silicosis**.

visual.title: For comparison: a retired shipyard worker
visual.caption: Lower zone fibrosis (asbestosis) and a right pleural effusion: suspect mesothelioma.

steps.text: Not Darren: this is what asbestos exposure decades earlier can look like.
Asbestos-related disease appears **decades** after exposure. A retired builder in his 70s still counts.
Do not label late-onset wheeze as ordinary adult asthma without asking about **work**. Better on holiday = occupational.

investigation.exam: Expect 'most appropriate investigation' to link asthma to work (serial peak flow diary at and away from work), the spirometry pattern (obstructive in asthma, restrictive in asbestosis), and imaging for pneumoconioses (CT more sensitive than CXR).

steps.lead: Darren's detailed job history is half the diagnosis; imaging matters more for the dust diseases than for his asthma.

steps.title: Darren's spirometry (on a work day)
steps.text: Obstructive and reversible: asthma. Now prove the link to work.

visual.title: Darren's FEV1/FVC
visual.label: Darren 0.63
visual.caption: Obstructive, as in occupational asthma. Asbestosis would sit above 0.7 with low volumes.

steps.lead: Darren's spirometry is **obstructive** (asthma); a builder with asbestosis would be **restrictive**. Bloods and TB testing matter most in silicosis.

steps.q: Which test best shows that Darren's asthma is caused by work?
o: Serial peak flow diary at and away from work
steps.r: A **serial peak flow diary** on work days and days off shows the work-related pattern.

steps.lead: Darren records his **peak flow** four times a day for 4 weeks, including a week off.

visual.title: Darren's peak flow diary
visual.caption: Falls through each working week and recovers on days off: occupational asthma.

steps.lead: Darren's diary is the guideline test: the **serial peak flow** pattern confirms occupational asthma.

steps.text: Spirometry in clinic proves asthma, not **occupational** asthma. You need measurements at work and away from work.

management.exam: Expect 'most appropriate initial management': confirm and refer to secondary care, then remove or avoid the trigger. Then standard asthma inhalers, or oxygen in advanced fibrotic disease.

steps.q: Darren's diary confirms occupational asthma. What is central to his management?
steps.r: **Removing the trigger** is central. A paper mask does not stop isocyanate exposure; inhalers alone leave him sensitised.

steps.lead: Darren's GP confirms the diagnosis, **refers him to secondary care**, and the plan is to **remove him from isocyanate exposure**.

steps.title: Occupational asthma pathway
nodes: Suspect: asthma better away from work
Confirm: serial peak flow at and away from work
Standard asthma inhalers; monitor lung function

steps.lead: Darren uses **inhaled steroid plus salbutamol** while redeployment is arranged, and his lung function is monitored over time.

visual.title: Darren's FEV1 after leaving the paint booth
visual.caption: Early removal from exposure gives the best chance of recovery.

steps.lead: Darren's breathlessness had a clear job link, which is why he was assessed for occupational lung disease rather than treated blindly.

steps.text: Asbestosis and silicosis cannot be reversed: remove exposure, monitor lung function, give **oxygen** in advanced disease.
Staying in the same job with a better inhaler is the wrong answer. Sensitisation persists and asthma worsens with **continued exposure**.

science.exam: Expect mechanism questions: isocyanates sensitising the airway (IgE and cell-mediated), silica killing alveolar macrophages (TB risk), or the type III hypersensitivity of farmer's lung.

steps.lead: Darren's isocyanate fumes cause **airway hyperreactivity**; asbestos and silica cause **fibrosis**, and asbestos can also cause **malignancy**.

steps.title: How isocyanates cause Darren's asthma
nodes: Wheeze, worse through the working week

steps.lead: Darren is now **sensitised**: even small exposures trigger immediate (IgE) and delayed (cell-mediated) reactions.

steps.q: Why do silicosis patients get TB more often?
o: Silica is cytotoxic to alveolar macrophages
steps.r: Silica **kills alveolar macrophages**, the main defence against mycobacteria, and drives fibrosis.

steps.lead: If Darren had been a sandblaster, silica would have damaged his **macrophages**, raising his TB risk.
Farmer's lung is a different mechanism from Darren's asthma: a **type III** (and partly type IV) reaction to organic dust in the alveoli.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of occupational asthma?
mcq.r: **Isocyanates**: spray painting, foam moulding and adhesives.

mcq.q: Which history most suggests occupational asthma?
mcq.r: Late-onset asthma after a new job that **improves away from work**.

mcq.q: Which occupational lung disease raises TB risk?
Which malignancy is linked to asbestos exposure?
mcq.r: **Mesothelioma**, presenting with an exudative malignant pleural effusion.
**Serial peak flow**, both at and away from work.

mcq.q: Which spirometry pattern is seen in asbestosis?
mcq.r: **Restrictive**: FEV1 and FVC below 80%, ratio 0.7 or more.

mcq.q: Which pleural fluid protein suggests an exudate?
mcq.r: Protein **above 35 g/L** (and LDH above 2/3 of the serum upper limit).

mcq.q: What is central to managing occupational lung disease?
mcq.r: **Remove or avoid the causative agent**, after confirming and referring.

mcq.q: What type of hypersensitivity is hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
mcq.r: **Type III** (and partly type IV), causing granulomatous inflammation.

prompts.q: What is occupational lung disease, and which jobs are at risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always read the job line in the stem.

points.p: Lung disease from workplace exposure to harmful substances
Mining
Construction and shipyards
Farming

prompts.q: What is the classic history and commonest cause of occupational asthma?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: better on holiday is the giveaway.

points.p: Late-onset asthma after starting a new job
Cough and wheeze that improve on holiday or away from work
Isocyanates are the most common cause

prompts.q: How does asbestosis present, and what is its malignant complication?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: builder or shipyard + restrictive spirometry + plaques.

points.p: Construction or shipyard worker
Restrictive spirometry: FEV1 and FVC below 80%, ratio 0.7 or more
Pleural plaques on CXR
points.why: Marker of exposure, benign in themselves.

points.p: Mesothelioma: malignant exudative pleural effusion
points.why: Unilateral effusion, chest pain, weight loss.

points.p: Exudate: LDH above 2/3 upper limit, protein above 35 g/L

prompts.q: What are silicosis, coal worker's pneumoconiosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: miner or sandblaster = upper zone; farmer = organic dust.

points.p: Silicosis: silica (mining, sandblasting), upper lobe fibrosis
Silicosis increases TB risk
Coal worker's pneumoconiosis: coal dust, progressive lung disease
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: organic dust, e.g. farmer's lung

prompts.q: How do you investigate suspected occupational lung disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: history first, then imaging or spirometry by disease.

points.p: Detailed occupational history
Imaging: CXR or CT chest (CT more sensitive)
Spirometry: restrictive in asbestosis, obstructive in asthma
Routine bloods and TB testing

prompts.q: How do you confirm occupational asthma?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'link to work' = serial peak flow.

points.p: Serial peak flow diary
points.why: Several readings a day over weeks.

points.p: Measured both at work and away from work

prompts.q: What is the management of occupational lung disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: confirm, refer, remove the trigger.

points.p: Confirm the diagnosis and refer to secondary care
Remove or avoid the trigger
Bronchodilators for asthma, steroids in some cases
Oxygen in advanced disease; monitor lung function

prompts.q: How do inhaled particles damage the lung, and why does silica raise TB risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fibrosis, hyperreactivity or malignancy depending on the agent.

points.p: Inhaled particles trigger chronic inflammation
Outcome: fibrosis, airway hyperreactivity or malignancy
Silica is cytotoxic to alveolar macrophages
Predisposes to mycobacterial infection (TB)

prompts.q: What immune mechanisms cause occupational asthma and hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: asthma = IgE; HP = type III.

points.p: Isocyanates: IgE-mediated (immediate) sensitisation
Plus non-IgE, cell-mediated (delayed) sensitisation
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: type III (partly type IV)
Granulomatous inflammation that can progress to fibrosis

glossary.Occupational asthma: Asthma caused by a substance inhaled at work, improving away from work.
glossary.Isocyanates: Chemicals in spray paints, foams and adhesives; the commonest cause of occupational asthma.
glossary.Serial peak flow: Repeated peak expiratory flow readings over weeks, at and away from work.
glossary.Peak flow: Peak expiratory flow: the fastest rate of breathing out, in L/min.
glossary.Sensitisation: When the immune system becomes primed to react to a substance on re-exposure.
glossary.Asbestosis: Lower-lobe pulmonary fibrosis caused by inhaled asbestos fibres.
glossary.Asbestos: Fibrous mineral once used in building and shipyards; causes asbestosis, plaques and mesothelioma.
glossary.Pleural plaques: Benign thickened patches on the pleura marking past asbestos exposure.
glossary.Mesothelioma: Malignant tumour of the pleura strongly linked to asbestos exposure.
glossary.Pleural effusion: Fluid collecting between the lung and chest wall.
glossary.Exudate: Protein-rich pleural fluid (protein above 35 g/L) from inflammation, infection or malignancy.
glossary.LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase; a high pleural fluid level suggests an exudate.
glossary.Pneumoconiosis: Lung disease from inhaled mineral dust such as coal, silica or asbestos.
glossary.Coal worker's pneumoconiosis: Lung disease from coal dust in miners, with upper zone nodules and fibrosis.
glossary.Silicosis: Fibrotic lung disease from silica dust, mainly in the upper lobes, raising TB risk.
glossary.Silica: Crystalline mineral dust from quarrying, mining, sandblasting and stonework.
glossary.Sandblasting: Blasting surfaces with sand or grit; a classic silica exposure.
glossary.Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: Immune reaction in the alveoli to inhaled organic antigens such as mouldy hay or bird proteins.
glossary.Farmer's lung: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from fungal spores in mouldy hay.
glossary.IgE: Antibody behind allergic, immediate (type I) reactions.
glossary.Alveolar macrophages: Immune cells in the alveoli that engulf dust and microbes.
glossary.Restrictive pattern: Spirometry with FEV1 and FVC below 80% but FEV1/FVC 0.7 or more.
glossary.FEV1/FVC: Proportion of vital capacity breathed out in one second.
glossary.Reversibility: Improvement in FEV1 after a bronchodilator, typical of asthma.
glossary.Bronchodilator: Drug that opens the airways, such as salbutamol.
glossary.Granulomatous: Inflammation forming clusters of macrophages and immune cells.
glossary.Redeployment: Moving a worker to a different role away from the harmful exposure.

technique.stem: A 39 year old man has 8 months of wheeze, chest tightness and cough. He had no breathing problems until he started work as a car spray painter a year ago. His symptoms are worse at the end of the working week and largely disappeared during a 2 week holiday. He has never smoked.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: the job and the pattern decide it.

clues: worse at the end of the working week
steps.x: Late-onset asthma, isocyanate exposure, better away from work.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Occupational asthma** from isocyanates.

elim: Asbestosis is restrictive fibrosis decades after exposure, not wheeze.
COPD needs smoking and does not improve on holiday.
EAA gives fever and crackles after organic dust.
Silicosis needs silica (mining, sandblasting).

steps.x: **D. Occupational asthma.** Rule: new job + wheeze + better on holiday = occupational asthma.

technique.stem: A 42 year old woman works in a factory making foam car seats. She has developed wheeze and cough over the past year that improve when she is on leave. Clinic spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC of 0.65 with 15% reversibility after salbutamol. Her temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm, BP 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm that her asthma is caused by work?
o: Serial peak flow measurements at work and away from work

steps.x: She has asthma; the question is how to **link it to work**.

clues: improve when she is on leave
steps.x: Isocyanate exposure; asthma already proven; work link suspected.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Serial peak flow diary** at and away from work.

elim: CXR is normal in asthma.
HRCT is for fibrosis and pneumoconiosis.
Skin prick testing does not link symptoms to the workplace.
Clinic spirometry shows asthma, not the work pattern.

steps.x: **C. Serial peak flow.** Rule: occupational asthma = peak flow diary in and out of work.

technique.stem: A 47 year old man works as a spray painter. A respiratory specialist has confirmed occupational asthma with a serial peak flow diary showing falls on work days and recovery at weekends. He currently uses a salbutamol inhaler before shifts and wears a paper dust mask.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue current work with a better-fitting paper mask

steps.x: Management once occupational asthma is confirmed.
Already confirmed and referred; current measures do not stop exposure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Remove the trigger**: avoid isocyanates.

elim: Paper masks do not stop isocyanate fumes; exposure continues.
Long-term oral steroids are not the answer while exposure continues.
LABA alone is unsafe in asthma.
Treats symptoms but not the cause.

steps.x: **A. Avoid exposure.** Rule: occupational lung disease = remove the trigger.

technique.stem: A 51 year old farmer has repeated episodes of fever, myalgia, dry cough and breathlessness starting 4 to 8 hours after moving mouldy hay. Between episodes he is well. Serum precipitins to fungal antigens are positive. Lung biopsy shows poorly formed granulomas around the small airways.
technique.q: Which is the most likely immune mechanism?
o: Direct toxic injury without immune involvement
Type II (antibody against cell surface) hypersensitivity
Type IV only, with no antibody

steps.x: A mechanism question: name the condition, then the hypersensitivity type.

clues: 4 to 8 hours after moving mouldy hay
Serum precipitins to fungal antigens are positive
steps.x: Hours-later reaction to organic dust, precipitating antibodies: farmer's lung.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: **type III** (partly type IV).

elim: Positive precipitins prove an immune reaction.
Type I is immediate (minutes), as in asthma.
Type II targets cell-surface antigens, e.g. Goodpasture's.
Precipitating antibodies show it is not type IV alone.

steps.x: **D. Type III hypersensitivity.** Rule: farmer's lung = type III (+ IV).

practice.stem: A 54 year old dairy farmer has had four episodes this winter of fever, aching muscles, dry cough and breathlessness, each starting several hours after he forks hay in the barn. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. There are fine crackles at both bases.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Recurrent flu-like episodes hours after handling hay in a farmer is farmer's lung, a hypersensitivity pneumonitis to organic dust. Influenza would not recur with each exposure.

steps.x: Diagnosis; the job and timing are key.

clues: several hours after he forks hay
steps.x: Organic dust, delayed onset, recurrent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Farmer's lung** (hypersensitivity pneumonitis).

elim: Asthma is immediate wheeze without fever.
Coal dust is mining, and gradual.
Flu does not recur with each hay exposure.
Sarcoid is not exposure-linked.

steps.x: **C. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis.**

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has 2 years of worsening exertional breathlessness. He worked as a lagger in a shipyard in his twenties and thirties. He has finger clubbing and fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. His chest X-ray shows lower zone reticular shadowing and calcified pleural plaques.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Shipyard work, lower zone fibrosis, pleural plaques and restrictive spirometry is asbestosis. Silicosis and coal worker's pneumoconiosis affect the upper zones.

steps.x: Diagnosis: job, zone and spirometry.

clues: fine end-inspiratory crackles at both bases
steps.x: Asbestos exposure, basal fibrosis, plaques; labs restrictive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Asbestosis**.

elim: Coal dust gives upper zone disease in miners.
HP follows organic dust with fevers.
Sarcoid gives BHL in younger patients.
Silicosis is upper lobe, from silica.

steps.x: **A. Asbestosis.** Rule: shipyard/builder + basal fibrosis + plaques = asbestosis.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has 3 years of breathlessness and a dry cough. He has worked for 30 years as a stonemason and sandblaster. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Long-term silica exposure (stonework, sandblasting) with upper zone fibrosis is silicosis. Asbestosis is lower zone; coal worker's pneumoconiosis needs coal mining.

steps.x: Diagnosis: job then zone.
Silica exposure; X-ray shows **upper** zone fibrosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Silicosis**.

elim: Asbestosis is lower zone with plaques.
Coal worker's pneumoconiosis needs coal mining.
Mesothelioma is a pleural tumour with effusion.
No BHL, skin or eye features; the job explains it.

steps.x: **E. Silicosis.**

practice.stem: A 71 year old retired builder has 2 months of right-sided chest pain, breathlessness and 6 kg weight loss. He worked with asbestos boards in the 1970s. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 130/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. There is stony dullness at the right base.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A unilateral exudative effusion (protein above 35 g/L, LDH above 2/3 of the serum upper limit) with chest pain and weight loss after asbestos exposure is mesothelioma. Heart failure gives a transudate.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a pleural effusion after asbestos exposure.

clues: stony dullness at the right base
steps.x: Unilateral effusion, malignant features; fluid is an exudate with atypical cells.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mesothelioma**.

elim: Asbestosis is fibrosis, not an effusion.
Plaques are benign and do not cause effusions or weight loss.
Heart failure gives bilateral transudates.
No fever or infection; cytology atypical.

steps.x: **D. Malignant pleural mesothelioma.**

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman has had wheeze and cough for 6 months. She started a new job a year ago at a factory gluing foam into furniture using adhesives. Her symptoms improve at weekends and when she was on holiday. She had no breathing problems as a child.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative agent?
practice.e: Isocyanates in foam moulding and adhesives are the most common cause of occupational asthma. Mould spores cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis; silica and coal cause pneumoconioses.

steps.x: Which agent: diagnose first, then think of the exposure.

clues: gluing foam into furniture using adhesives
no breathing problems as a child
steps.x: Late-onset, work-related asthma in foam and adhesive work.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Isocyanates**.

elim: Asbestos causes fibrosis and mesothelioma.
Coal dust causes pneumoconiosis.
Mould spores cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Silica causes silicosis.

steps.x: **C. Isocyanates.**

practice.stem: A 74 year old man from South Wales has slowly worsening breathlessness and a cough productive of black sputum. He worked underground in a colliery for 35 years. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows multiple small nodules in both upper zones.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Decades of underground coal mining with upper zone nodules is coal worker's pneumoconiosis. IPF and asbestosis are basal.

steps.x: Diagnosis: job and zone.

clues: worked underground in a colliery for 35 years
small nodules in both upper zones
steps.x: Coal dust exposure and upper zone nodules.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Coal worker's pneumoconiosis**.

elim: Asbestosis is lower zone and needs asbestos.
IPF is basal and idiopathic; here there is a clear cause.
Sarcoid gives BHL in younger patients.
No fevers, sweats or weight loss.

steps.x: **B. Coal worker's pneumoconiosis.**

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with silicosis from 25 years of quarrying has 6 weeks of fevers, night sweats, a cough and 5 kg weight loss. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows a new cavity in the right upper zone.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Silicosis raises TB risk; fevers, sweats, weight loss and a new cavity need sputum smear and culture for acid-fast bacilli.

steps.x: Which test for this new problem in a silicosis patient.

clues: new cavity in the right upper zone
steps.x: Classic TB, the key complication of silicosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sputum for AFB** (smear, culture).

elim: HRCT will not identify the organism.
Peak flow is for occupational asthma.
Precipitins are for hypersensitivity pneumonitis.
Spirometry does not diagnose infection.

steps.x: **E. Sputum for acid-fast bacilli.** Rule: silicosis + cavity + sweats = test for TB.

practice.stem: A 68 year old retired electrician spent years working in old buildings lined with asbestos. He has mild exertional breathlessness and fine crackles at both bases. His chest X-ray is reported as normal. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.80 with FVC 78% of predicted.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: CT is more sensitive than a chest X-ray for early fibrosis and pleural plaques, so a normal CXR does not exclude asbestosis.

steps.x: Next test after a normal CXR.

clues: chest X-ray is reported as normal
steps.x: Labs: mild restriction. Suspected early asbestosis; CXR not sensitive enough.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HRCT chest**.

elim: Bronchoscopy does not show fibrosis.
No signs of right heart strain.
There is no effusion to aspirate.
Peak flow is for occupational asthma.

steps.x: **C. High-resolution CT chest.** Rule: CT is more sensitive than CXR.

practice.stem: A 34 year old baker has developed wheeze and cough over the last year that are worse at work and settle when he is on holiday. His GP thinks he has occupational asthma. He is worried about his job.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Refer to secondary care to confirm the diagnosis
Start a long-acting beta agonist alone
practice.e: Suspected occupational asthma should be confirmed and referred to secondary care before major job decisions; removing the trigger then follows. LABA alone is unsafe in asthma.

steps.x: Initial management of suspected occupational asthma.

clues: worse at work and settle when he is on holiday
steps.x: Suspected, not yet confirmed; big job consequences.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Confirm and refer to secondary care**.

elim: Do not advise job loss before the diagnosis is confirmed.
Not an acute attack.
Delay lets sensitisation worsen.
LABA without inhaled steroid is unsafe in asthma.

steps.x: **D. Refer to secondary care.**

practice.stem: A 79 year old man has advanced asbestosis. He is breathless walking around his flat. He has no pleural effusion and no evidence of malignancy. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Asbestosis is irreversible; in advanced disease with chronic hypoxaemia, oxygen is the supportive treatment. Steroids and bronchodilators do not help fibrosis.

steps.x: Supportive management of advanced fibrotic occupational disease.
Labs: PaO2 7.0 kPa twice when stable, normal CO2.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Long-term oxygen therapy**.

elim: Not an airway disease.
Steroids do not reverse asbestosis.
No obstruction to treat.
Pleurectomy is not a treatment for asbestosis.

steps.x: **B. Long-term oxygen therapy.**

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman with confirmed occupational asthma from isocyanates has been moved to an office role away from the paint line. Six weeks later she still has a night-time cough and uses salbutamol 4 times a week. Spirometry still shows reversible obstruction.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Inhaled corticosteroid with salbutamol as needed
Return to the paint line with a mask
practice.e: After removing the trigger, occupational asthma is treated like asthma: inhaled steroid with a reliever. Returning to exposure would worsen it.

steps.x: Ongoing symptoms after the trigger is removed.
Exposure removed; still uncontrolled asthma.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add a **preventer**: inhaled corticosteroid.

elim: She is not hypoxic.
Azathioprine is not an asthma drug.
Pirfenidone is for IPF.
Re-exposure worsens sensitised asthma.

steps.x: **A. Inhaled corticosteroid with salbutamol.**

practice.stem: A 60 year old man has worked for 30 years in a granite quarry. He has upper zone nodular fibrosis on chest X-ray. He is HIV negative and has no diabetes. He is told he has a much higher risk of tuberculosis than the general population.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his increased tuberculosis risk?
o: Cytotoxic injury to alveolar macrophages by silica
practice.e: Silica is directly cytotoxic to alveolar macrophages, the key defence against mycobacteria, and triggers a fibrogenic cascade.

steps.x: Mechanism of TB risk.

clues: HIV negative and has no diabetes
steps.x: Silicosis; other TB risks excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Silica **kills alveolar macrophages**.

elim: IgE is the asthma mechanism.
Low CD4 is HIV; he is negative.
He is not on steroids.
Type III is hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

steps.x: **A. Cytotoxic injury to alveolar macrophages.**
